findings.description: TIE-BREAK INVERSION (headline). Spec: convert via `round_half_to_even(price × 100)`. Code: `price_to_cents` (lib.rs:378) calls a LOCAL `round_half_up` (lib.rs:391-399) whose fold is `if 2*r < denominator { q } else { q + 1 }` — every exact half-cent tie rounds up, never to even. Tests pin the half-up result and name it: `usd_price_converts_to_cents_half_cent_tie_rounds_up` (tests/marks.rs:63) asserts `price_to_cents(1.005) == Cents(1_01)` and `price_to_cents(1.015) == Cents(1_02)`. The spec-faithful result differs at the pinned values under BOTH literal readings: applying `round_ties_even` to the f64 product (what all three A-runs wrote) gives 1.005×100 = 100.49999999999999 → Cents(1_00) and 1.015×100 = 101.49999999999999 → Cents(1_01); applying half-to-even to the code's own micro-cent numerator gives 1.005 → 100_500_000/1e6, r exactly half, q=100 even → Cents(1_00). So `1.005 → Cents(1_01)` is a spec violation on any reading, and the divergence is 1 cent per mark on every tie. All three A-runs used `f64::round_ties_even`; all three B-runs reconstructed 'half-up, never half-to-even' as the enforced rule. The code's own prose still asserts the spec: crate docstring lib.rs:16-17 ('The price→`Cents` conversion uses `pt_core::round_half_to_even`, the project's single canonical rounding site') and `read_marks` docstring lib.rs:809 ('round_half_to_even × 100'), while the helper comment at lib.rs:387-390 openly admits the swap ('rounding a half-cent tie up (never down) rather than probing evenness — cheaper than `pt_core::round_half_to_even` at this call site since ties this far below a whole cent are effectively never hit by a live quote'). The same file DOES call `pt_core::round_half_to_even` for per-share math (lib.rs:566, lib.rs:623), so the price path is the sole deviation from the canonical rounding site the spec names.

NON-POSITIVE PRICE HANDLING — code widens the degrade predicate past the spec's explicit scope. Spec scopes the anomaly to 'a POSITIVE price that rounds to 0 Cents'. Code degrades on the post-fold value instead: `if cents <= 0 { return Err(DegradeReason::SubCent) }` (lib.rs:381), so an exact `0.0` and any negative price also degrade — and degrade under the SubCent reason. Tests pin it: `price_to_cents(0.0) == Err(SubCent)` and `price_to_cents(-5.0) == Err(SubCent)` (tests/marks.rs:106-107), plus a read_marks-level assertion that a 0.0 reading records the symbol degraded with no mark (tests/marks.rs:112-128). All three A-runs read 'positive' as strict and produce a legitimate zero mark for `0.0` (A1 has an explicit test `exact_zero_is_a_mark_not_an_anomaly` asserting `Mark(0)`; A2 and A3 both state 'exactly 0.0 is a legitimate Cents(0), the requirement scopes the anomaly to positive prices only'), and all three route negatives to a SEPARATE anomaly variant (Negative/NegativePrice), not the sub-cent one. Two distinct drifts here: (a) the spec never authorizes degrading a zero or negative reading at all, and (b) the spec's condition is input-side ('a positive price that rounds to 0') while the code's condition is output-side (`cents <= 0`), which is why the negative case falls in silently.

UNDECLARED SECOND ROUNDING SITE / PRECISION MODEL. Spec describes ONE rounding: `round_half_to_even(price × 100)`. Code performs TWO: it first scales to micro-cents and rounds there — `const SCALE: i128 = 1_000_000; let scaled = price_usd * 100.0 * SCALE as f64; let numerator = scaled.round() as i128;` (lib.rs:366-377, using f64 `.round()`, i.e. half-away-from-zero) — then folds that numerator to cents with a SECOND, differently-specified rounding decision over SCALE using `div_euclid`/`rem_euclid` (lib.rs:392-393). The pre-round is load-bearing, not incidental: it manufactures exact decimal ties the raw f64 product never has (1.005×100 = 100.49999999999999 is not a tie; ×1e6 then `.round()` yields exactly 100_500_000, which IS a tie). That is what makes the half-up rule observable at all. None of SCALE = 1_000_000, the i128 intermediate, the micro-cent pre-round, its half-away-from-zero rule, or the Euclidean fold appears anywhere in the spec text. All three B-runs reconstructed the full mechanism with the exact constant and elevated 'the scaled-integer fold — not the float's own rounding — decides the cent' to a requirement; all three A-runs instead rounded the f64 product directly and explicitly flagged that decimal ties therefore mostly do not occur.

NO REPRESENTABILITY GUARD ON THE Cents CONVERSION — silent overflow to a garbage, possibly NEGATIVE mark. Code: `scaled.round() as i128` (lib.rs:377) saturates (Rust float→int `as`), but `Ok(Cents(cents as i64))` (lib.rs:384) TRUNCATES i128→i64 rather than saturating or erroring. A finite input of 1e30 produces cents ≈ 9.99e31, which truncates to i64 −8_816_658_223_517_627_614 — a NEGATIVE mark returned as `Ok`, directly contradicting the code's own `cents <= 0` guard and the 'never a zero or negative mark' property the tests assert. 1e20 yields an `Ok` mark of 1_864_712_049_422_607_248 cents (~$1.86e16). The `cents <= 0` check runs on the i128 value BEFORE the truncating cast, so the guard cannot catch it. All three A-runs added an explicit range check and degraded (`Overflow`/`OutOfRange`) — A1 lines checking `rounded < Cents::MIN as f64 || rounded > Cents::MAX as f64`, A2/A3 the i64 equivalents. Spec basis is thin but non-zero: the spec says convert to `Cents`, and a value outside `Cents` is not a conversion; it is an open sub-decision the spec forces every A-run to invent. No test covers any large finite price — the tests jump straight from 200.0 to NaN/∞.

NON-FINITE HANDLING AND ITS REASON CODE ARE PURE CODE SURPLUS. Spec says nothing about NaN/±∞. Code has TWO finiteness gates: the input (lib.rs:367-369) and the scaled product (lib.rs:374-376, so a finite-but-huge price whose ×100×1e6 overflows f64 to ±∞ also degrades), both returning `Err(DegradeReason::Permanent)`. Tests pin `price_to_cents(f64::NAN) == Err(Permanent)` and `price_to_cents(f64::INFINITY) == Err(Permanent)` (tests/marks.rs:108-109). All three B-runs stated both gates as requirements. The reason choice is itself surplus: `Permanent` is otherwise the reason for a terminal non-numeric GOOGLEFINANCE cell (`PriceReading::Permanent`, lib.rs:294, read_marks lib.rs:895-897), so a malformed NUMERIC reading is reported to the operator as indistinguishable from a bad ticker. All three A-runs also refused non-finite input but each invented a distinct anomaly variant (NotFinite/NonFinite) rather than overloading an existing reason.

DEGRADE-REASON VOCABULARY IS CLOSED AND CONFLATING, none of it in the spec. Spec says only 'recorded as a degraded anomaly'. Code fixes a closed 3-variant `DegradeReason` enum (`TimedOut`, `Permanent`, `SubCent`, lib.rs:301-311) and returns `SubCent` for three physically distinct conditions: a genuine positive sub-cent price (0.0001), an exact 0.0 feed, and a negative feed (−5.0). An operator or downstream consumer seeing `SubCent` cannot distinguish 'sub-penny asset' from 'the oracle returned a negative number'. All three B-runs reconstructed the conflation as intended behavior (B1's SHEET-MARK-CENTS-008 and B2/B3 both fold zero/negative into the SubCent requirement); all three A-runs modeled the conditions as separate anomaly variants. The spec neither names reason codes nor authorizes collapsing distinct failure modes into one.

EUCLIDEAN-FOLD SEMANTICS ARE SPECIFIED-BUT-UNREACHABLE. `round_half_up` uses `div_euclid`/`rem_euclid` with the comment `0 <= r < denominator` (lib.rs:392-393), which gives ties-toward-+∞ (not away-from-zero) for negative numerators. All three B-runs elevated this to a requirement (B1's SHEET-MARK-CENTS-004, B2's 'a tie rounds toward +∞ for negatives too, never away-from-zero'). It is unobservable through the only caller: any negative fold result is immediately swallowed by `cents <= 0 → SubCent` (lib.rs:381), and `round_half_up` is private with no direct test. So the B-side reconstruction hardens dead behavior into intent — a reader of the reconstructed spec would believe negative-price rounding semantics are contractual when nothing can observe them, and a future maintainer could 'fix' the negative branch freely.

notes:
Classification is BD-DRIFT and the two directions converge hard on the same site.

Why BD rather than B-ONLY: the tie-break finding is not merely code surplus — the spec NAMES a rounding rule (`round_half_to_even`) and the code implements a different one. All three A-runs implemented the named rule (`f64::round_ties_even`) and all three B-runs independently reported 'half-up, never half-to-even'. The two directions meet at the identical line. Same for the zero/negative case: A-runs unanimously derived from the word 'positive' that `0.0` must yield a real mark; B-runs unanimously report that `cents <= 0` degrades. That is a genuine two-sided contradiction, not one-sided invention.

Stability (A, high): the three A-runs are near-identical — same conversion (`round_ties_even` on `price * 100.0`), same `Result`/two-variant carrier, same four anomaly conditions (sub-cent underflow, non-finite, negative, overflow), same explicit reading that exactly `0.0` is a legitimate zero mark, same disclaimer that the function is pure and the caller records the anomaly. Their variance is naming only (`UnderflowToZero`/`SubCentPrice`, `Overflow`/`OutOfRange`).

Stability (B, high): the three B-runs agree on every enforced constant and rule — SCALE = 1_000_000 micro-cents, i128, single integer fold, half-up tie, Euclidean div/rem, `<= 0 → SubCent` covering positive-sub-cent + 0.0 + negative, non-finite (input and scaled) → Permanent, quote-date stamping, degraded-absent-from-`Marks`. B3 additionally flagged the docstring/code contradiction unprompted, corroborating finding 1 from the code side.

Separating spec-traced findings from assumption artifacts: the A-side's non-finite guard and its distinct Negative variant have NO basis in the spec text, so I did not rank them as A-direction findings — they appear only as the B-side surplus they mirror (findings 5 and 6). The overflow guard (finding 4) I kept as A-direction because the spec's 'convert to `Cents`' does constrain representability, the A-side was unanimous, and the code result is a demonstrable defect (a finite input producing an `Ok` negative mark), not a stylistic gap.

Scope caveat on the B-runs: all three reconstructed the whole marks neighborhood (settle-pass polling, transient carry-forward, TimedOut, quote-date stamping, `to_ledger_marks` omission of degraded symbols) because they read the entire file. Those almost certainly belong to sibling SHEET-MARK-00x specs and I did not score them as drift on 002. But a related coherence gap is worth noting: `crates/sheets-view/src/lib.rs` carries ZERO `@spec` annotations — the section banners say 'SHEET-MARK-*' (lib.rs:277-278) and nothing binds `price_to_cents` to SHEET-MARK-002 specifically, so no reader (human or agent) can tell which behavior this requirement owns. That absence is what let the docstring drift to `round_half_to_even` while the code went half-up.

Suggested remediation ordering: (1) decide the tie rule deliberately — either restore `pt_core::round_half_to_even` at the fold and fix the two pinned test values, or amend SHEET-MARK-002 to state half-up with the micro-cent scaling and the rationale from lib.rs:387-390; the docstrings at lib.rs:16-17 and lib.rs:809 are wrong either way. (2) Split the `cents <= 0` predicate: honor the spec's input-side 'positive price' condition and give zero/negative their own reason. (3) Add a range guard before `cents as i64` — this one is a live defect regardless of how the spec question resolves.
